pgtelegraph.focus.key_help: SPACE or left mouse = key   |   ESC = leave
pgtelegraph.focus.paddle_help: Dit: Z / Left / left mouse   Dah: X / Right / right mouse   |   ESC = leave
pgtelegraph.tooltip.failure: Burns out on over-voltage, over-current or overheating
A _straight key_ that connects its two terminals while held. Acts as a _switch_ in the circuit.
When R-Click is held with an empty hand
_Focus mode_: key with Space or Left Mouse
block.pgtelegraph.paddle.tooltip.summary: A paddle with a centre _common (COM)_ terminal and _dit/dah_ contacts on each side. No timing of its own - wire it to an _Electronic Keyer_.
block.pgtelegraph.paddle.tooltip.conditi: When R-Clicked with an empty hand
block.pgtelegraph.keyer.tooltip.summary: Iambic keyer that turns paddle input into _correctly timed_ dits and dahs. An internal _5 V supply_ senses the inputs through pull-ups.
block.pgtelegraph.keyer.tooltip.conditio: When a paddle shorts DIT/DAH to COM
block.pgtelegraph.keyer.tooltip.behaviou: Closes the _output contact_ (OUT1-OUT2) in Morse timing. Squeezing both _alternates_
block.pgtelegraph.sounder.tooltip.summar: Receiver whose armature goes _click_ when current flows and _clack_ when it stops - read by ear on wired telegraph lines.
block.pgtelegraph.sounder.tooltip.behavi: The armature _pulls in_; it _releases_ below 0.07 A
block.pgtelegraph.relay.tooltip.summary: Uses the _weak current_ of a long line to close a contact, so a _local battery_ can drive the sounder hard.
block.pgtelegraph.relay.tooltip.conditio: When the rear coil reaches the pick-up current
block.pgtelegraph.relay.tooltip.behaviou: The _front contact_ closes; opens below 70% of the setting
block.pgtelegraph.buzzer.tooltip.summary: Gives a steady _beep_ while current flows. Good for receiving practice.
pgtelegraph.tape.occupied: There is already a tape inside
pgtelegraph.tape.inker_rejects: The inker only takes blank or inked tape
pgtelegraph.tape.blank_rejected: A blank tape has nothing to send
pgtelegraph.perforator.help: Letters, digits or Hangul; Enter = punch
block.pgtelegraph.inker.tooltip.summary: Records the received signal as an _ink line on paper tape_. The clockwork starts with the first mark and stops after _3 s_ of silence.
block.pgtelegraph.inker.tooltip.behaviou: Loads the tape; an inked tape is _continued_
block.pgtelegraph.inker.tooltip.conditio: When R-Clicked with an empty hand
block.pgtelegraph.inker.tooltip.behaviou: Takes the tape out. Right-click the tape to see the trace and _decoded text_
The ink wheel drops and _draws a line_. Up to 10 minutes per tape
block.pgtelegraph.perforator.tooltip.sum: Wheatstone-style perforator: type a message and get tape _punched in Morse_. Needs no power.
block.pgtelegraph.perforator.tooltip.con: When R-Clicked with blank paper tape
block.pgtelegraph.perforator.tooltip.beh: Opens the input box. _Letters, digits and Hangul_ (Korean Morse), up to 120 characters
block.pgtelegraph.tape_transmitter.toolt: A star wheel reads the tape and works the _output contact_. Needs a _Create shaft on the back, sides or bottom_ to pull the tape.
_Starts sending_ at once. Punched tape runs at _RPM/4 WPM_ (up to the front governor, 5-24 WPM); inked tape plays _as received at 48 RPM_. _Stalls below 8 RPM_, _tears above 128 RPM_
When R-Clicked with an empty hand
_Pause / resume_. Sneak R-Click takes the tape out
item.pgtelegraph.paper_tape.tooltip.summ: Telegraph tape. Load it into an _Inker_ to record, or punch a message on a _Perforator_.
item.pgtelegraph.paper_tape.tooltip.cond: When R-Clicked holding a recorded tape
item.pgtelegraph.paper_tape.tooltip.beha: Unrolls it, with the text _decoded in English and Korean_
block.pgtelegraph.switchboard.tooltip.su: 8-line board that _patches lines together with cords_. Any number of cords at once; wire line terminals between boards to chain _several boards with trunks_.
block.pgtelegraph.switchboard.tooltip.co: Holding insulated copper wire, right-click two jacks in turn
block.pgtelegraph.switchboard.tooltip.be: Patches the _two lines together_ with one wire. Picking the same two jacks again with an empty hand pulls the cord and gives the wire back
block.pgtelegraph.switchboard.tooltip.co: Sneak + empty hand on a jack
block.pgtelegraph.switchboard.tooltip.be: Pulls _every cord_ out of it (wires back) and resets its drop
block.pgtelegraph.switchboard.tooltip.co: When 5 mA or more arrives on an idle line
block.pgtelegraph.switchboard.tooltip.be: Its _drop shutter_ falls (orange). The rear _common terminal_ must be grounded
block.pgtelegraph.transmitter.tooltip.su: Transmitter with modes _CW / FSK (RTTY) / AM / FM / SSB_ (button in the tuning screen). In CW and FSK it is keyed by the KEY terminals; in AM or FM a _microphone_ next to it keys it while someone talks. Draws real power from its supply, and the antenna has to be _matched_. SSB (upper sideband) sends voice with no carrier - the HF voice mode; a receiver needs a 2.4 kHz filter for it, and a slight mistuning shifts the voice up or down.
block.pgtelegraph.transmitter.tooltip.co: When R-Clicked with an empty hand
block.pgtelegraph.transmitter.tooltip.be: Opens the _dial_ (type kHz, band buttons, wheel = 100 Hz)
Output _1-100 W_ at 13.8 V; lower voltage gives less. 60% efficient
block.pgtelegraph.transmitter.tooltip.co: When keyed without an antenna or at high SWR
block.pgtelegraph.transmitter.tooltip.be: Reflected power _overheats_ it. Reversed supply polarity burns it too
block.pgtelegraph.receiver.tooltip.summa: Receiver with modes _CW / FSK / AM / FM / SSB_. CW: signals within ±1.5 kHz as a _700 Hz + offset_ tone, OUT closes on a signal in the 500 Hz filter. AM (6 kHz) / FM (12.5 kHz): _plays the voice_ of a transmitter in the same mode; FM is silent below the squelch and clean above ~14 dB SNR, AM gets steadily noisier as it weakens. SSB (upper sideband) sends voice with no carrier - the HF voice mode; a receiver needs a 2.4 kHz filter for it, and a slight mistuning shifts the voice up or down. The tuning screen has the front-panel knobs: _ATT_ 0/10/20 dB against overload, _AGC_ fast/slow/off, _NB_ noise blanker for clicks and crashes, and _FIL_ to narrow the fitted filter (CW 500/250 Hz, SSB 2.4/1.8 kHz).
block.pgtelegraph.receiver.tooltip.condi: When R-Clicked with an empty hand
block.pgtelegraph.receiver.tooltip.behav: Wire a sounder, inker or relay to _copy radio traffic_. Threshold = front _squelch_ (SNR dB)
block.pgtelegraph.antenna_rod.tooltip.su: 1 m of antenna conductor. _Stack up_ from the feed for a vertical (about 75 / length MHz) or _extend both ways_ for a dipole (about 150 / total length MHz).
block.pgtelegraph.antenna_rod.tooltip.be: 40 m (7 MHz): _10-11_ vertical or _21_ dipole. 20 m (14 MHz): _5_ vertical or _11_ dipole
One-block _1 m antenna_. Far too short for HF: very high SWR and loss (about -30 dB at 7 MHz).
block.pgtelegraph.coax_thin.tooltip.summ: Coax laid like redstone, 1 block = 1 m. Loss _0.046 dB/m_ at 10 MHz (scales with the square root of f), max _200 W_ - more burns it. Click the _side_ of a block to clip it to the wall: it then runs straight up and down, joins cable above and below, and goes over the top onto cable lying there.
block.pgtelegraph.coax_thick.tooltip.sum: Thick coax. Loss _0.022 dB/m_ at 10 MHz, max _1500 W_. Click the _side_ of a block to clip it to the wall: it then runs straight up and down, joins cable above and below, and goes over the top onto cable lying there.
Rigid low-loss hardline. Loss _0.011 dB/m_ at 10 MHz, max _3000 W_. Click the _side_ of a block to clip it to the wall: it then runs straight up and down, joins cable above and below, and goes over the top onto cable lying there.
block.pgtelegraph.linear_amplifier.toolt: Tube amplifier with _20 dB (x100)_ gain: _100 W in, 10 kW out_. Runs on high voltage, so only a few amps flow. _Coax after it must take the power_: thick 1.5 kW, hardline 3 kW, heavy 20 kW - an overloaded run burns through at its weakest piece.
Transmitter → coax → amplifier → coax → antenna, on _any sides_ (it finds which run leads to the antenna). Rear lower _HV_ (2400 V), upper _filament_ (12.6 V, about 55 W)
Amplifies after _30 s warm-up_ (the tube glows). Before that, or below 1000 V plate, it is in _bypass_
_Output limit_ 100 W - 10 kW. 65% efficient: 10 kW means ~5 kW of heat. _Create fans_ help
block.pgtelegraph.coax_heavy.tooltip.sum: Large hardline for kilowatt stations. Loss _0.006 dB/m_ at 10 MHz, max _20 kW_. Click the _side_ of a block to clip it to the wall: it then runs straight up and down, joins cable above and below, and goes over the top onto cable lying there.
pgtelegraph.coil.no_mast: No vertical mast connected by coax
pgtelegraph.coil.help: Watch the resonance with goggles and bring it onto your frequency. Wheel = 0.2%
block.pgtelegraph.loading_coil.tooltip.s: A huge coil that _resonates an electrically short mast at LF / VLF_. Wire transmitter → _coax_ → coil → _coax_ → mast. Merely placing it next to the mast does not connect it.
block.pgtelegraph.loading_coil.tooltip.c: When R-Clicked with an empty hand
block.pgtelegraph.loading_coil.tooltip.b: Sets the _inductance (mH)_. Goggles show _resonance, bandwidth and efficiency_
Part of the loss _heats the coil_. VLF bandwidth is _~100 Hz_: a small error sends the SWR up
Umbrella wire from the mast top, 1 block = 1 m. Connects _diagonally_ too, so ribs can slope down. More wire = more _capacitance and effective height_ (about 3x the mast height is plenty).
block.pgtelegraph.ground_mat.tooltip.sum: Buried copper ground mesh. The more within _24 blocks_ of the mast foot (4 up/down), the lower the _ground loss_ - the biggest factor in VLF efficiency.
block.pgtelegraph.broadcast_amplifier.to: Broadcast-class tube stage: _20 dB_, output limit _1-200 kW_. Plate _10 kV_, filament _48 V / 2.4 kW_, _60 s_ warm-up. Drive it from a linear amplifier (1-2 kW). _Output coax: rigid line_ (500 kW) - heavy coax only takes 20 kW and burns through above that.
block.pgtelegraph.alexanderson_alternato: Makes RF _directly by rotation_, no tubes. Create shaft into the back. _Frequency = RPM x 67.19 Hz_ (256 RPM = 17.2 kHz, the Grimeton frequency).
_200 kW_ at 256 RPM, scaling with speed squared. The _key terminals_ on top switch the field for CW. Stress _256 SU/RPM_
A speed change _moves the frequency_ off the antenna's resonance. Keep the speed steady
block.pgtelegraph.vhf_whip.tooltip.summa: Omni ground-plane whip for VHF/UHF, _2.15 dBi_. Band on the side Create panel (6 m - 23 cm).
block.pgtelegraph.yagi_antenna.tooltip.s: Directional Yagi: _12 dBi_, _40°_ beam, _20 dB_ front-to-back. Band on the side panel, aim with an _empty-hand right-click_.
block.pgtelegraph.dish_antenna.tooltip.s: 1 m parabolic dish, _1-30 GHz_. Gain rises with frequency (about 38 dBi and a 2° beam at 10 GHz) - aim it _precisely_.
block.pgtelegraph.dish_antenna.tooltip.c: When R-Clicked with an empty hand
block.pgtelegraph.dish_antenna.tooltip.b: Opens the _azimuth / elevation_ rotator. 'Where I look' copies your view direction
block.pgtelegraph.yagi_antenna.tooltip.c: When R-Clicked with an empty hand
block.pgtelegraph.yagi_antenna.tooltip.b: Opens the _azimuth / elevation_ rotator. It is placed pointing where you look
block.pgtelegraph.helical_whip.tooltip.s: 1 m whip _helically wound_ to resonate on an HF band (mobile style). Band on the side panel (160 m - 6 m). Short, so less efficient: ~23% on 20 m, ~7% on 40 m, ~0.5% on 160 m, and narrow.
block.pgtelegraph.receiving_loop.tooltip: _Tuned receiving loop_ for kHz - 30 MHz (10 turns, 1 m²). Very inefficient, but LF/VLF atmospheric noise is so strong that it _hears about as well as a huge antenna_. It can transmit, but barely radiates.
When R-Clicked with an empty hand
Sets the _tuning frequency_ (match your receiver). Narrow
Sets its _direction_. Maximum in the loop plane, _a deep null broadside_ (figure-eight) - turn it to find a station's bearing
Axial-mode helix for UHF/SHF (1 m long, circular polarisation). Band on the side panel (23 cm - 3 cm), aim with an empty-hand right-click. About 18 dBi and an 18° beam at 2.3 GHz.
pgtelegraph.handheld.help: Hold right-click to key (CW)  -  wheel = 1 kHz
Dual-band 2 m (144-148 MHz) / 70 cm (430-440 MHz) _handheld CW transceiver_. Rubber duck (~-5 dBi), _0.5 / 1 / 5 W_, _7.4 V 2 Ah (14.8 Wh)_ battery.
_Transmits_ while held, like a key. In _paddle mode_ (switch it on the panel) _left = dit, right = dah_ through the _built-in keyer_. Sneak + wheel = speed
Receives from _anywhere in the inventory_ (in hand: frequency, S-meter, battery). _Higher ground_ reaches further. 0.4 W on receive, 10 W while sending 5 W
block.pgtelegraph.handheld_charger.toolt: Charges a handheld from a 12 V Power Grid supply at _about 10 W_ (9 V or more, 85% efficient). Empty to full in about 1 h 45 min.
R-Click with the radio / with an empty hand
_Dock / take_. Green light with a radio docked, red when empty
pgtelegraph.part.deep: Deep-discharged - charging it may cause thermal runaway!
pgtelegraph.handheld.runaway: Battery thermal runaway! Throw it away now!
item.pgtelegraph.screwdriver.tooltip.sum: Right-click an installed radio (transmitter, receiver) to open its _parts bay_. Handhelds open theirs from the panel's Parts button.
What is left of a radio after its battery ran away. Nothing inside is usable.
pgtelegraph.tape_tx.torn: The shaft is too fast - the tape tore! (over 128 RPM)
pgtelegraph.tape_tx.no_drive: No rotation - the tape is stopped (needs 8 RPM or more)
pgtelegraph.tape_tx.too_fast: Too fast! The tape will tear (keep it at 128 RPM or less)
block.pgtelegraph.litz_loading_coil.tool: A _premium loading coil_ wound from hundreds of fine insulated strands. Little skin-effect loss: _Q 3000_ (plain coil 800), about _twice the VLF efficiency_. Wired like the plain coil: transmitter → _coax_ → coil → _coax_ → mast.
When R-Clicked with an empty hand
Opens the _inductance (mH)_ dial. Tune it while watching _resonance, bandwidth and efficiency_ through Engineer's Goggles
Lower loss means _less heat_, but the bandwidth gets narrower: _tune more precisely_
block.pgtelegraph.keyer_paddle.tooltip.s: A paddle with an _iambic keyer built into its base_. Runs on an internal cell: _no supply needed_. The two _OUT terminals_ at the back close in Morse timing, like the keyer's output.
block.pgtelegraph.keyer_paddle.tooltip.c: When R-Clicked with an empty hand
block.pgtelegraph.keyer_paddle.tooltip.b: _Focus mode_: Z/←/left mouse = dit, X/→/right mouse = dah. Squeeze both to _alternate_
Sets the speed, _5-40 WPM_. The output contact is rated _30 V, 0.5 A_: switch heavy loads through a _relay_
item.pgtelegraph.clip_key.tooltip.summar: A key you carry and _clip onto any two terminals_ with test leads, like a multimeter. No block, no wiring: _cut into a line_ anywhere. The contact is part of the real circuit (_250 V, 3 A_).
item.pgtelegraph.clip_key.tooltip.behavi: Clips the leads on _one at a time_ (1, then 2). Sneak + R-Click the _air_ to take both off
The leads are _shorted_ while held. Put it away to open; walk more than _12 blocks_ off and the leads come loose. Overloading it _burns the contact_
item.pgtelegraph.clip_paddle.tooltip.sum: A _keyer paddle_ on test leads. Clip it onto two terminals and the keyer output closes between them (_30 V, 0.5 A_).
item.pgtelegraph.clip_paddle.tooltip.beh: Clips the leads on _one at a time_. Sneak + R-Click the _air_ to take both off
_Left mouse = dit_, _right mouse = dah_. Sneak + _wheel_ = speed (5-40 WPM)
pgtelegraph.clip.same: That is the terminal lead 1 is on
pgtelegraph.clip.pulled: Walked too far: the leads came off
pgtelegraph.clip.lost: The terminal is gone: the lead came off
pgtelegraph.handheld.paddle_help: Paddle %s WPM: left = dit, right = dah, sneak + wheel = speed
block.pgtelegraph.dummy_load.tooltip.sum: A _50 Ω resistor in oil_. Connect coax to it instead of an antenna to test a transmitter _without radiating_ (leaks about -60 dB).
block.pgtelegraph.dummy_load.tooltip.beh: All power turns into heat: _6 kJ/K_, cools _10 W/K_. Smokes above _120 °C_, the resistor opens at _180 °C_. 100 W settles ~10 °C above air, _1.5 kW_ continuous settles near 170 °C, 5 kW burns it in ~3.5 min.
A desk automatic tuner for the coax run, like most shack tuners: matches the antenna up to _SWR 10:1_. Its loss grows with the mismatch (0.3 dB matched, about 1.4 dB at 10:1) and the coax _between it and the antenna_ still runs at the antenna's SWR. Past 10:1 it gives up - use a _remote tuner at the antenna_ or a _manual tuner_.
block.pgtelegraph.beacon.tooltip.summary: Small transmitter (_1-25 W_, 13.8 V) that keys itself from a program. _{CALL}_ in the message becomes the station callsign.
block.pgtelegraph.beacon.tooltip.behavio: Program: _message_ (repeat with a pause), _NDB_ (8 s carrier + ident, for direction finders) or _carrier_.
The beacon stays _silent_ (a clock or relay can switch it).
block.pgtelegraph.solar_beacon.tooltip.s: Self-contained beacon for remote hills: _5 W solar panel_, _20 Wh battery_, _0.1-5 W_ output. Needs open sky. Coax on any side.
block.pgtelegraph.solar_beacon.tooltip.b: Tune / program. At 1 W key-down most of the time it runs _~30 h_ on a full battery; full sun charges it in _~5 h_.
block.pgtelegraph.spark_transmitter.tool: 1900s style: a spark gap rings the antenna. _No oscillator_ - the signal sits on the _antenna's own resonance_, smeared over _10 %_ of it (at least 20 kHz), heard as a rasp across the band.
_1 kV_ nominal (needs _≥400 V_, insulation _3 kV_), panel _up to 2 kW_, efficiency _25 %_. The dial does nothing.
block.pgtelegraph.repeater.tooltip.summa: Hears the _dial frequency_ and re-sends it mark for mark on _dial + offset_ (HF +100 kHz, VHF +600 kHz, UHF +5 MHz, >1 GHz +12 MHz). One antenna, built-in duplexer. Up to _50 W_.
block.pgtelegraph.repeater.tooltip.behav: Sends _DE call/R_ every 10 minutes while idle.
block.pgtelegraph.oscilloscope.tooltip.s: Two channels (_CH1+/-_, _CH2+/-_), _1 MΩ_ inputs rated _1 kV_, one sample per tick, last _10 s_ kept. Empty hand: open the screen.
block.pgtelegraph.bms.tooltip.summary: Between a pack (_BAT+/-_) and the load or charger (_LOAD+/-_). A MOSFET opens on _under-voltage_, _over-voltage_ or _over-current_ (panel settings).
block.pgtelegraph.bms.tooltip.behaviour1: The MOSFET fails _short_ - as real ones do - and the pack is _no longer protected_.
block.pgtelegraph.decoder.tooltip.summar: A _100 Ω_ coil (pulls in at _10 mA_) times the marks and spaces; after _2 s_ of silence it writes the text. Wire it like a sounder, or to a receiver's OUT.
block.pgtelegraph.decoder.tooltip.condit: Empty hand / sneak / book and quill
block.pgtelegraph.decoder.tooltip.behavi: Show the text / switch _English-Korean_ / copy the text into the book.
block.pgtelegraph.teleprinter.tooltip.su: Typewriter on a wire: _ITA2_ 5-bit code at _10 baud_ (~1.25 chars/s). _TX 1/2_: sending contact. _RX 1/2_: 100 Ω magnet (10 mA). Line idles _open_, so it also works over an on-off keyed radio.
block.pgtelegraph.telegraph_pole.tooltip: Stack it, then put an _insulator_ or _wooden peg_ on top to hold an overhead wire.
block.pgtelegraph.glass_insulator.toolti: Tie point for a wire. Leaks to earth: dry _50 MΩ_, in rain _50 kΩ_.
block.pgtelegraph.wooden_peg.tooltip.sum: Cheap tie point. Leaks to earth: dry _50 kΩ_, in rain only _400 Ω_ - a long line on pegs goes dead in a storm.
block.pgtelegraph.lightning_arrester.too: Gas tube in the coax run. Lightning within _6 blocks_ of an antenna burns every radio down its coax - unless the surge meets a _grounded_ arrester first.
A Power Grid _grounding rod_ or a _ground mat_ touching it, or two blocks below it.
block.pgtelegraph.rotator.tooltip.summar: Vertical _shaft from below_ turns the beam antenna on top (yagi, dish, helix, loop) through a _100:1_ worm. _64 RPM_ ≈ one turn in _2.5 min_. Stress _1 SU/RPM_.
item.pgtelegraph.meter.swr.hint: Hold and look at a transmitter: forward, reflected, SWR
item.pgtelegraph.meter.field.hint: Hold: total RF arriving here, all frequencies
item.pgtelegraph.meter.counter.hint: Hold: frequency of the strongest signal (above -90 dBm)
item.pgtelegraph.meter.df.hint: Hold and sweep: signal strength in the 40° beam. Sneak + use: tune
item.pgtelegraph.repair_kit.hint: Use on a burnt device: new coils and contacts. One use.
item.pgtelegraph.license.hint: Name it in an anvil = callsign. Use on a beacon or repeater to sign it.
item.pgtelegraph.qsl_card.blank: Blank - fill it from a logbook entry
pgtelegraph.beacon.title: Beacon program
pgtelegraph.battery.li_ion.hint: No protection of its own: overcharge = fire. Use a BMS.
pgtelegraph.battery.lifepo4.hint: Safe chemistry: abused it vents and dies, no fire.
pgtelegraph.battery.lead_acid.hint: Overcharge gasses off water; left flat it sulphates.
pgtelegraph.elt.triggered: Impact! Your ELT switched itself on (121.5 MHz).
pgtelegraph.logbook.no_card: You need a blank QSL card
pgtelegraph.cipher.key: Key: rotors (1-5 x3), start letters, plug pairs  e.g. 152 KQX AB CD
block.pgtelegraph.launch_pad.tooltip.sum: Faces _the way you look_ when placed - that is the _launch azimuth_: east gives the lowest inclination (= latitude 37.5°), north/south a _polar_ orbit, west a retrograde one. Needs open sky.
block.pgtelegraph.launch_pad.tooltip.con: Rocket, then CubeSat, then empty hand
block.pgtelegraph.launch_pad.tooltip.beh: _10 s_ countdown (or a redstone pulse); _5 %_ blow up on the pad. Small rocket: _500-800 km_ (passes every 16 min of play, decays in hours to days). Medium: _1200-2000 km_ (longer passes, lasts). Heavy: _geostationary_ - parked over this longitude, always up (elevation ~46° south). Sneak + empty hand unloads.
item.pgtelegraph.cubesat.hint: Use: set up everything it does in orbit
item.pgtelegraph.meter.tracker.hint: Hold: the satellite overhead (az/el, range, beacon Doppler) or the next pass
pgtelegraph.launch.failed: Launch failure - the rocket exploded on the pad
pgtelegraph.launch.orbit: %s is in orbit: %s | %s km, inclination %s°, period %s min (%s min of play)%s
pgtelegraph.launch.need_rocket: Put a rocket on the pad first
pgtelegraph.launch.not_ready: Needs a rocket and a CubeSat
pgtelegraph.cubesat.name: Name
pgtelegraph.cubesat.hint: Text tokens: {NAME} {LAT} {LON} {SFI} {KP} {MUF} {FOF2} {FLARE}. In orbit: RTTY uplink "SET KEY VALUE" ANT OMNI/EARTH/SPOT, SPOTLAT/SPOTLON (deg).
block.pgtelegraph.ionosonde.tooltip.summ: Sweeps 1-20 MHz straight up through _any antenna on its coax_ every 5 s and draws the _ionogram_: echo height against frequency. Shows _foE, foF2, MUF, fmin_, Kp and flares. Empty hand: open.
block.pgtelegraph.qso_robot.tooltip.summ: A _5 W_ CW transceiver with its own operator: answers _CQ ... DE call_, answers calls to its callsign with a report, signs off after _TU_ or _73_, calls CQ every 5 min when quiet. Coax to an antenna. License = its callsign.
Records what a _receiver touching it_ plays onto a _magnetic tape_ (5 min) and plays it back. Tape in hand: load. Empty hand: stop → record → play. Sneak: eject.
block.pgtelegraph.coax_switch.tooltip.su: Common port at the _back_ (toward you when placed), port _A left_, port _B right_. No redstone: A; redstone: B. Pick one of two antennas (or radios) remotely.
block.pgtelegraph.phased_array.tooltip.s: Lay tiles side by side; coax to any one. N tiles: _5 + 10 log N dBi_, beam _100°/√N_ (16 tiles: 17 dBi, 25°; 64 tiles: 23 dBi, 12.5°; 256: 29 dBi, 6°). Steered electronically - aim it like a yagi (also at the moon or a satellite). Band on the fed tile's panel.
block.pgtelegraph.sstv_monitor.tooltip.s: FM receiver (3 kHz) with a picture tube: tuned to a satellite's or a ground _SSTV transmitter_'s frequency it paints the _320×256 picture_ line by line (51 s). Grain fades out by about _30 dB SNR_; weaker gives streaks and sideways shear, below _3 dB_ nothing. _Below 30 MHz (SSB) tune exactly_: 100 Hz off = 12 % brighter/darker, 600 Hz off = no lock. _From 30 MHz (FM)_ an offset is harmless until past 1.2 kHz, then only noisier. Sky-wave signals flutter and ghost. _Paper in hand_: print the screen as a photo. The picture also shows on the monitor's own screen as it comes in - no need to open it.
_Plays a record on the air_ in _AM_ (an imported recording or any music disc, looping), _150 kHz-30 MHz_: long, medium and short wave. Up to _1 kW_ carrier, supply 250 V (min 120 V), 70 % efficient. A _microphone_ next to it goes out live over the record. INHIBIT shorted to COM takes it off the air. Radios join the record where the station is.
Add to the playlist (up to 9, played in turn) / Take out the last one added
block.pgtelegraph.broadcast_radio.toolti: Radio with a loudspeaker. _Below 30 MHz AM_ (9 kHz): quieter and noisier as the signal weakens. _Above 30 MHz FM_ (200 kHz): clean when strong, crackles near the threshold, hisses between stations. Built-in ferrite rod (-20 dB); coax to an outside antenna is far better. Empty hand: on/off, sneak: tune. Default 1000 kHz.
item.pgtelegraph.blank_record.hint: Use: import an MP3, WAV or OGG file from your computer (up to 8 min)
pgtelegraph.record.need_blank: Hold the blank record until the upload finishes
pgtelegraph.sat.reentry: %s re-entered the atmosphere and burned up
pgtelegraph.contest.start: Contest on for %s minutes. Log the exchange (report + serial, e.g. 5NN 012). Score = QSOs x multipliers (callsign prefixes HL1, JA2 ...)

advancement.pgtelegraph.rtty.desc: Have a teleprinter print a message
advancement.pgtelegraph.dx500.desc: Hear a station 500 km or more away

block.pgtelegraph.microphone.tooltip.sum: Put it _against a transmitter set to AM or FM_ (or a broadcast transmitter). Within _4 blocks_, hold _push-to-talk (V)_ and talk into your _real microphone_: the transmitter keys up and receivers in the same mode play your voice. The microphone is only open while the key is held.
block.pgtelegraph.tv_camera.tooltip.summ: Looks the way _you faced when placing it_ (70° view, 64 blocks deep, 320×256). Touching an _SSTV transmitter_ it is the _live picture_, scanned line by line as it goes out, in the blocks' real texture colours. Empty hand: tilt _-45° to +45°_. Changed resource pack? Type _/pgtexture_.
block.pgtelegraph.sstv_transmitter.toolt: A transmitter (same parts, supply and antenna as the CW one) that sends a _320×256 colour picture_, 0.2 s a line, _51 s_ a frame. Picture: the _photo_ put on it, or else the _TV camera_ touching it. Starts when a photo goes on, on _sneak + empty hand_, or while _KEY_ is shorted (held: frame after frame). Default _14.230 MHz_. Receive with an _SSTV receiver_. Modes (tuning screen): Martin M1/M2, Scottie S1/S2, Robot 36 and PD50-PD290 with their real resolutions (up to 800 x 616) and frame times; for PD pick the resolution and the speed. Slower modes survive weaker signals. The receiver picks the mode up from the VIS header by itself.
Photo in hand / sneak + empty hand
Put it on (sends at once) / take it off, or send a camera frame

item.pgtelegraph.camera.tooltip.summary: Takes a _320×256 photo_ of exactly what you see (without your hand and the HUD), on _one sheet of paper_ from your inventory. Put the photo on an _SSTV transmitter_ to send it.

block.pgtelegraph.coax_rigid.tooltip.sum: Broadcast-station rigid line: a copper pipe inside a copper pipe, gas-filled (the 6-1/8 inch class). Loss _0.003 dB/m_ at 10 MHz, max _500 kW_. What a high-power broadcast amplifier feeds its antenna through. Click the _side_ of a block to clip it to the wall: it then runs straight up and down, joins cable above and below, and goes over the top onto cable lying there.

pgtelegraph.ponder.sstv_station.text_1: A hand camera takes a 320x256 photo of what you see, on one sheet of paper
pgtelegraph.ponder.sstv_station.text_2: Put the photo on the SSTV transmitter - or let a TV camera touching it send a live picture
pgtelegraph.ponder.sstv_station.text_3: It sends a line every 0.2 s, 51 s a frame - like any transmitter it needs power and an antenna
pgtelegraph.ponder.sstv_station.text_4: An SSTV receiver on the same frequency paints it line by line. Paper in hand prints the screen
pgtelegraph.ponder.sstv_station.text_5: Below 30 MHz tune exactly: 100 Hz off shifts the brightness. Sky-wave pictures flutter and ghost
pgtelegraph.ponder.high_power.text_1: Amplifiers go in the coax run. Any side works: the side whose coax leads to the antenna is the output
pgtelegraph.ponder.high_power.text_2: Each stage adds 20 dB: 100 W -> linear amplifier 10 kW -> broadcast amplifier up to 200 kW
pgtelegraph.ponder.high_power.text_3: Every coax has a power rating: thin 200 W, thick 1.5 kW, hardline 3 kW, heavy 20 kW, rigid line 500 kW
pgtelegraph.ponder.high_power.text_4: Overload a run and its weakest piece burns through. Each stage needs coax rated above its output
pgtelegraph.ponder.auto_stations.text_1: A repeater hears its dial frequency and re-sends it on dial + offset (HF +100 kHz, VHF +600 kHz, UHF +5 MHz). One antenna, up to 50 W
pgtelegraph.ponder.auto_stations.text_2: Signed with a license, it sends DE call/R every 10 minutes while idle
pgtelegraph.ponder.auto_stations.text_3: A QSO robot is a 5 W CW station with its own operator: call CQ and it answers with a report, and signs off after TU or 73
pgtelegraph.ponder.auto_stations.text_4: A beacon keys itself from a program (sneak + empty hand): a message, an NDB for direction finders, or a carrier
pgtelegraph.ponder.auto_stations.text_5: A solar beacon needs no supply: 5 W panel, 20 Wh battery, 0.1-5 W out. Give it open sky
pgtelegraph.ponder.auto_stations.text_6: Each still needs coax to an antenna
pgtelegraph.ponder.voice_station.text_1: Set the transmitter to AM or FM (button in the tuning screen)
pgtelegraph.ponder.voice_station.text_2: Put a microphone against it. Within 4 blocks, hold push-to-talk (V) and talk into your real microphone
pgtelegraph.ponder.voice_station.text_3: Receivers in the same mode play your voice. FM is clean above about 14 dB SNR; AM gets steadily noisier as it weakens
pgtelegraph.ponder.voice_station.text_4: A tape recorder touching the receiver records 5 minutes onto magnetic tape. Empty hand: stop -> record -> play
pgtelegraph.ponder.switchboard.text_1: A switchboard takes 8 lines. Holding insulated copper wire, right-click two jacks in turn: one wire becomes the cord. The same pair again with an empty hand pulls it and gives the wire back.
pgtelegraph.ponder.switchboard.text_2: A call - 5 mA or more on an idle line - drops that line's orange shutter
pgtelegraph.ponder.switchboard.text_3: The rear common terminal must be grounded
pgtelegraph.ponder.switchboard.text_4: Sneak + empty hand on a jack pulls every cord out of it. Wire line terminals of two boards together for a trunk.
pgtelegraph.ponder.radio_basics.text_1: A radio station is three things: a radio, a feed line (coax) and an antenna
pgtelegraph.ponder.radio_basics.text_2: Frequency and wavelength go together: wavelength (m) = 300 / frequency (MHz). 7 MHz is the 40 m band, 14 MHz the 20 m band
pgtelegraph.ponder.radio_basics.text_3: An antenna works best at resonance. Rods stacked up from the feed make a vertical: about 75 / length MHz (5 rods = 15 MHz)
pgtelegraph.ponder.radio_basics.text_4: Rods extended both ways from the feed make a dipole: about 150 / total length MHz (11 rods = about 14 MHz)
pgtelegraph.ponder.radio_basics.text_5: A wrong length reflects power back (high SWR) and overheats the transmitter. An antenna tuner in the coax fixes the match
pgtelegraph.ponder.radio_basics.text_6: Every metre of coax loses a little, more at higher frequency: keep runs short and use thicker coax for long ones
pgtelegraph.ponder.decibels.text_1: Radio power is counted in decibels: +3 dB = twice the power, +10 dB = 10 times, +20 dB = 100 times
pgtelegraph.ponder.decibels.text_2: So 100 W instead of 10 W is only +10 dB - a better antenna or a quieter band often helps more
pgtelegraph.ponder.decibels.text_3: The S-meter shows signal strength: S9 = -73 dBm, each S-unit is 6 dB. Engineer's Goggles show it on a receiver
pgtelegraph.ponder.decibels.text_4: What decides whether you can copy is signal over noise (SNR). Noise is highest on low bands, at night and in thunderstorms
pgtelegraph.ponder.decibels.text_5: Narrow modes win: CW in a 500 Hz filter lets in about 11 dB less noise than AM (6 kHz)
pgtelegraph.ponder.propagation.text_1: Low frequencies (LF / MF) follow the curve of the ground: the ground wave. Its loss grows with frequency
pgtelegraph.ponder.propagation.text_2: On HF (3-30 MHz) the signal bounces off the ionosphere - the sky wave - and can reach far across the world
pgtelegraph.ponder.propagation.text_3: Only below the MUF (maximum usable frequency): about 20 MHz by day and 10 MHz at night at an average sun
pgtelegraph.ponder.propagation.text_4: By day the D layer swallows the low bands: use about 14-21 MHz by day and 3.5-7 MHz at night
pgtelegraph.ponder.propagation.text_5: Close to the MUF there is a skip zone: too far for the ground wave, too near for the sky wave
pgtelegraph.ponder.propagation.text_6: Above 30 MHz (VHF / UHF) it is line of sight: height matters most - put antennas high, or go through a satellite
pgtelegraph.ponder.propagation.text_7: Geomagnetic storms lower the MUF and solar flares black out the low HF by day for a few minutes. The ionosonde shows it all
block.pgtelegraph.fm_broadcast_transmitt: _Plays a record on the air_ in _FM_ (75 kHz deviation, 75 us pre-emphasis), _87.5-108 MHz_ built in - no band module needed. Up to _1 kW_, supply 250 V (min 120 V), 65 % efficient. VHF goes as far as line of sight: _put the antenna high_. Microphone and INHIBIT as on the AM set. Radios join the record where the station is.
Add to the playlist (up to 9, played in turn) / Take out the last one added

pgtelegraph.radio.missing_parts: Missing parts: %s - open it with a screwdriver and fit them
block.pgtelegraph.tv_transmitter.tooltip: Sends the _live picture of a TV camera_ touching it, like a television station. _54-890 MHz_ (VHF / UHF TV) built in, up to _1 kW_ from 250 V. The camera is filmed by a nearby player's game - the _real view_, 640 x 480; with nobody near, a coarse stand-in. INHIBIT shorted to COM takes it off the air.
block.pgtelegraph.tv_receiver.tooltip.su: Shows a TV station on its screen. A weak or obstructed signal looks like analog TV: _snow_, colour fading, _ghosts_ behind hills, lines tearing and the picture _rolling_, bars from another station on the channel. Coax to an outside antenna beats its rabbit ears. Empty hand: watch close up; sneak: change channel.

item.pgtelegraph.bodycam.tooltip.summary: A camera worn in the _chest armour slot_, paired with an _analog TV transmitter_. Worn within 300 blocks of it, it films _what you actually see_ (your own game view, 640 x 480, 10 frames a second) and the transmitter puts it on the air in place of a TV camera block. Sneak + R-click a TV transmitter: pair. R-click: put it on.
pgtelegraph.bodycam.paired: Paired with the TV transmitter at %s
pgtelegraph.bodycam.unpaired: Not paired: sneak + R-click a TV transmitter
pgtelegraph.video.hold_tape: Hold a video tape (or a camcorder with a tape, not recording) in your main hand
pgtelegraph.video.no_file: No such file. Put video files in %s
pgtelegraph.camcorder.no_tape: No tape (sneak + R-click with a tape in the off hand)
item.pgtelegraph.video_tape.tooltip.summ: Holds _10 minutes_ of video at 320 x 240, 15 frames a second (about VHS). Recorded by a _VCR_ or a _camcorder_, or filled from a video file on the server's machine with _/pgvideo import_ (_/pgvideo export_ saves it back out as MP4; both need ffmpeg on the server).
item.pgtelegraph.camcorder.tooltip.summa: Records _what you see_ onto the tape inside it while you hold it. Sneak + R-click with a tape in the off hand: load it. Sneak + R-click with an empty off hand: take the tape out. R-click: record / stop.
block.pgtelegraph.vcr.tooltip.summary: Plays and records video tapes. Empty hand: _STOP > PLAY > LOOP > REC_. Recording goes on _after what is already on the tape_ and starts after a second, so clicking past REC records nothing. Sneak + empty hand: eject. To wipe a tape, hold it and sneak + use it twice in the air. Playing, its RF output puts the picture on channel 3 (61.25 MHz).
pgtelegraph.vhf.dish_band: Broadband 1-30 GHz: no band to set (gain rises with frequency)
block.pgtelegraph.speaker: Loudspeaker
pgtelegraph.amp.source: Fed by the radio set touching it
pgtelegraph.speaker.reach: Heard out to about %s m on its axis
block.pgtelegraph.audio_amplifier.toolti: Plays the sound of a _radio set touching it_ (broadcast radio or receiver) through the loudspeakers wired to its _SPK_ terminals. _1-2000 W_ out, from _230 V_ on PWR (60 % efficient: 1 kW out takes about 1.7 kW). The output is shared between the speakers on the line.
block.pgtelegraph.speaker.tooltip.summar: A cone loudspeaker: _92 dB at 1 m for 1 W_, up to _100 W_ (112 dB). Broad: 6 dB quieter to the side, 12 dB behind. Wire its two terminals to an audio amplifier's SPK terminals (or stand it against the amplifier). Driven past 150 W for 5 s it burns out.
block.pgtelegraph.horn_speaker.tooltip.s: A long-range horn loudspeaker, the kind used across a border: _112 dB at 1 m for 1 W_, up to _600 W_ (140 dB), in a _15 degree beam_ from the mouth at its back. Each speaker is heard by the physics: 6 dB less per doubling of distance, about 5 dB a km to the air, and late by the time sound takes (343 m/s). Empty hand: tilt. _Dangerous_: from 120 dB (within about 10 m in front at full power) it hurts, and 110 dB makes you queasy; a wall or a helmet helps.
death.attack.pgtelegraph.loudspeaker: %1$s was deafened to death by a loudspeaker
death.attack.pgtelegraph.loudspeaker.pla: %1$s was deafened to death by a loudspeaker
pgtelegraph.speaker.too_loud: %s dB - it hurts! Get out of the beam
block.pgtelegraph.jammer.tooltip.summary: Sends _noise_ instead of a signal: its power spread over a chosen _bandwidth_ (10 kHz - 50 MHz) round the dial. Receivers there do not hear a station - their _noise floor rises_ and weak signals drown first. Narrower = harder (+10 dB per tenth of the width). Up to _1 kW_ from 250 V (with parts fitted like a transmitter); jams radios, TV sets, SSTV monitors and satellites listening for commands. INHIBIT shorted to COM: off. Find it with a directional antenna.
item.pgtelegraph.manpack_radio.tooltip.s: A two-way _NFM_ field radio worn on the back (_chest armour slot_). Same parts and battery as a handheld, but _1-20 W_ and a _1 m whip_ above the shoulder - several times the range. Hold _V_ (push to talk) to speak; whoever is on the frequency comes through the earpiece with real noise and squelch. R-click: put it on. Sneak + R-click: settings and parts.
pgtelegraph.lna.burnt: LNA burnt out (transmitted into) - replace it
block.pgtelegraph.inline_lna.tooltip.sum: A low-noise amplifier for the _coax run_, best _right at the antenna_: _+20 dB_, noise figure _0.8 dB_. The signal is lifted before the long coax can lose it, so weak VHF/UHF stations come up out of the hiss. On HF the sky is noisier than any amplifier - it gains nothing there. It only amplifies towards the radio: _transmit through it and it burns out_ (40 dB loss until replaced) - give the transmitter its own antenna or a coax switch.
pgtelegraph.ponder.radio_station.text_1: A CW transmitter puts out 1-100 W (front panel) at 13.8 V, about 60 % efficient: 100 W out draws about 170 W
pgtelegraph.ponder.radio_station.text_2: Its supply goes on the back PWR+ / PWR- terminals (Power Grid wire). Reversed polarity burns it
pgtelegraph.ponder.radio_station.text_3: A key across the front KEY / COM terminals keys the carrier
pgtelegraph.ponder.radio_station.text_4: RF leaves through coax on any free side. A desk antenna tuner in the run matches up to SWR 10:1, a remote tuner at the antenna up to 100:1, and a manual tuner 64:1 at the frequency its knobs are set for; the worse the match, the more they lose
pgtelegraph.ponder.radio_station.text_5: Coax is laid like redstone, 1 block = 1 m. Thin coax loses about 0.05 dB/m at 10 MHz and carries at most 200 W
pgtelegraph.ponder.radio_station.text_6: A lightning arrester stops surges - but only when a ground mat or a Power Grid grounding rod touches it (or sits two blocks below)
pgtelegraph.ponder.radio_station.text_7: Lightning within 6 blocks of the antenna burns every radio down an unprotected coax
pgtelegraph.ponder.radio_station.text_8: To test without radiating, put a dummy load where the antenna was: a 50 Ohm resistor in oil
pgtelegraph.ponder.radio_station.text_9: All the power becomes heat: 100 W settles about 10 C above air, 1.5 kW near 170 C. Above 180 C the resistor opens
pgtelegraph.ponder.battery_bms.text_1: Three packs: Li-ion 4S 20 Ah (12.0-16.8 V), LiFePO4 4S 50 Ah (10.0-14.6 V, flat near 13.3 V), lead-acid 12 V 100 Ah
pgtelegraph.ponder.battery_bms.text_2: Each has a current limit: Li-ion 40 A, LiFePO4 100 A, lead-acid 200 A. More than that for a second cooks the pack
pgtelegraph.ponder.battery_bms.text_3: A pack has no protection of its own. Overcharged, Li-ion catches fire and explodes, LiFePO4 vents and dies, lead-acid gasses and loses capacity
pgtelegraph.ponder.battery_bms.text_4: Put a BMS between the pack and everything else: BAT+ / BAT- (back) go to the pack
pgtelegraph.ponder.battery_bms.text_5: LOAD+ / LOAD- (front) go to the radio - and the charger goes there too, so charging is protected as well
pgtelegraph.ponder.battery_bms.text_6: Its front panel sets the under-voltage and over-voltage cut-off and the current limit; a MOSFET opens when one is crossed
pgtelegraph.ponder.battery_bms.text_7: Lead-acid left nearly flat slowly sulphates and loses capacity - keep it charged
pgtelegraph.ponder.battery_bms.text_8: Above 100 A its MOSFET fails short - after that, nothing protects the pack
pgtelegraph.ponder.overhead_line.text_1: Stack telegraph poles and put a glass insulator or a wooden peg on top: that is where the line wire is tied
pgtelegraph.ponder.overhead_line.text_2: Run Power Grid wire from tie point to tie point (up to 16 blocks per span)
pgtelegraph.ponder.overhead_line.text_3: Sending end: battery + to the key, the key to the line. Battery - goes to a grounding rod
pgtelegraph.ponder.overhead_line.text_4: Receiving end: line to the decoder (or a sounder), then to a second grounding rod. The earth carries the current back - one wire is enough
pgtelegraph.ponder.overhead_line.text_5: The decoder pulls in at 10 mA, times the marks and spaces, and writes the text after 2 s of silence
pgtelegraph.ponder.overhead_line.text_6: In rain every tie point leaks to earth: a glass insulator 50 MOhm dry, 50 kOhm wet...
pgtelegraph.ponder.overhead_line.text_7: ...a wooden peg 50 kOhm dry but only 400 Ohm wet. A long line on pegs goes dead in a storm
pgtelegraph.ponder.overhead_line.text_8: On a long line use glass, a higher battery voltage, or a relay at the far end (see Wired telegraph)
pgtelegraph.ponder.overhead_line.text_9: A teleprinter types over the same kind of line: ITA2 code at 10 baud. TX 1/2 is its sending contact, RX 1/2 a 100 Ohm magnet (10 mA)
pgtelegraph.ponder.satellite_station.tex: First set up a CubeSat (use it): name, TX power and payloads - CW beacon, transponder, RTTY, SSTV, mailbox, ionosonde
Put a rocket on the pad, then the CubeSat, then an empty hand starts the 10 s countdown (or a redstone pulse). 5 % blow up on the pad
Small rocket: 500-800 km, a pass every 16 min, decays in hours to days. Medium: 1200-2000 km, lasts. Heavy: geostationary, always up
The pad's facing is the launch direction: east for the lowest orbit, north or south for a polar one
Put the yagi on a rotator and drive it with a shaft from below (here a cogwheel): 100:1, 64 RPM is about one turn in 2.5 min
Set the antenna to 'Aim: satellite': it follows the pass and corrects the radio for Doppler
Hold a Satellite Tracker to see the satellite overhead (azimuth / elevation, range, beacon Doppler) or the next pass
Receivers hear the beacon and transponder; an SSTV receiver paints the satellite's pictures of the Earth
Satellites are above 30 MHz, so it is line of sight: you hear one only while it is above the horizon
pgtelegraph.ponder.broadcast.text_1: Use a blank record to import an MP3, WAV or OGG file - it becomes a recorded disc
pgtelegraph.ponder.broadcast.text_2: Put the record (or any music disc) on the broadcast transmitter: it plays it on the air, looping. Sneak + empty hand takes it off
pgtelegraph.ponder.broadcast.text_3: It needs a 250 V supply (works from 120 V) and gives up to 1 kW carrier, 70 % efficient - 1 kW out draws about 1.4 kW
pgtelegraph.ponder.broadcast.text_4: It broadcasts AM from 150 kHz to 30 MHz: long, medium (530-1700 kHz) and short wave. By night medium wave reaches far off the ionosphere
pgtelegraph.ponder.broadcast.text_5: For FM there is the blue FM broadcast transmitter: 87.5-108 MHz built in, clean wide audio, but only as far as line of sight - put its antenna high
pgtelegraph.ponder.broadcast.text_6: Like any transmitter it needs coax to a matched antenna. Medium wave wants a tall mast - or a tuner
pgtelegraph.ponder.broadcast.text_7: A microphone next to it goes out live over the record. INHIBIT shorted to COM takes it off the air
pgtelegraph.ponder.broadcast.text_8: The station is the clock: its record keeps turning on the air. A radio switched on 30 s into a song joins it 30 s in, like a real broadcast
pgtelegraph.ponder.broadcast.text_9: A radio tuned to its frequency plays the programme. Empty hand: on / off, sneak: tune (starts at 1000 kHz)
pgtelegraph.ponder.broadcast.text_10: What you hear went through the air: AM sounds narrow (up to 4.5 kHz) and gets quieter and noisier as it weakens; FM is wide and clean, then crackles near the threshold
pgtelegraph.ponder.broadcast.text_11: Its built-in ferrite rod is 20 dB down: coax to an outside antenna hears far better
pgtelegraph.ponder.cw_station.text_1: A transmitter has four wire terminals: PWR+ / PWR- on the back, KEY / COM on the front. Look at it to see their names
pgtelegraph.ponder.cw_station.text_2: Power first: battery + to PWR+, battery - to PWR-, with Power Grid wire. 13.8 V gives full power; reversed polarity burns it
pgtelegraph.ponder.cw_station.text_3: 100 W out draws about 12 A: any of the battery packs can do it (Li-ion up to 40 A)
pgtelegraph.ponder.cw_station.text_4: Then the key: one terminal to KEY, the other to COM. Holding the key closes them and the carrier goes out (CW mode)
pgtelegraph.ponder.cw_station.text_5: Anything that closes a contact can key it instead: an electronic keyer's OUT, a tape transmitter, a relay contact
pgtelegraph.ponder.cw_station.text_6: Last, coax from any free side to a matched antenna. Never key without one: the reflected power overheats it
pgtelegraph.ponder.cw_station.text_7: Empty hand on it opens the dial: type the frequency in kHz or pick a band
pgtelegraph.ponder.cw_station.text_8: A receiver is wired the same way: power on the back, coax to an antenna. Tune it to the same frequency to hear the tone
pgtelegraph.ponder.cw_station.text_9: Its front OUT contact closes while a signal is heard. Put it in a loop with a battery and a decoder, sounder or inker: battery + -> device -> OUT -> OUT -> battery -
pgtelegraph.ponder.cw_station.text_10: The squelch on its front panel sets how strong a signal must be to close OUT. Engineer's Goggles show the S-meter and SWR
pgtelegraph.ponder.operating.text_1: The station: battery to PWR+ / PWR- (back), key to KEY / COM (front), coax to an antenna. "Wiring a CW station" shows it step by step
pgtelegraph.ponder.operating.text_2: Name a Station License in an anvil: that is your callsign. Use it on a beacon or repeater to sign it
pgtelegraph.ponder.operating.text_3: To find a contact, call CQ: CQ CQ DE <your call> K. Whoever hears you answers with their callsign
pgtelegraph.ponder.operating.text_4: Exchange an RST report: Readability 1-5, Strength 1-9, Tone 1-9. 599 is perfect
pgtelegraph.ponder.operating.text_5: Common shorthand: QTH = location, QSL = received / confirm, QRZ = who is calling?, TU = thank you, 73 = best regards
pgtelegraph.ponder.operating.text_6: Write each contact in the Station Logbook (call, frequency, RST, note); a logbook entry fills in a blank QSL card
pgtelegraph.ponder.operating.text_7: Nobody else on the air? A QSO robot answers your CQ - good practice
pgtelegraph.ponder.wired_telegraph.text_: A telegraph key is only a switch: its two terminals are joined while you hold it. It needs a battery and a receiver in one loop
Simplest line: battery + -> key -> sounder -> back to battery -. 12 V through the 20 Ohm sounder is 0.6 A
The sounder pulls in at 0.1 A (click) and drops below 0.07 A (clack): you read the gaps between click and clack
Real lines save the return wire: ground both ends with a Power Grid grounding rod and the earth carries the current back
Earth adds resistance: conductive blocks around a grounding rod lower it
A long line is too weak for a sounder. Put a relay at the far end: the line goes through its rear coil (150 Ohm)
It picks up at 5-200 mA (top panel, default 20 mA) and lets go below 70 % of that
Its front contact is a switch for a local loop: local battery + -> contact -> contact -> sounder -> battery -. Now the sounder clicks hard
For practice a buzzer (100 Ohm, beeps from 10 mA, 400-1000 Hz) can take the sounder's place
Sneak R-click the key for focus mode: key with Space or the left mouse button
pgtelegraph.ponder.keyer.text_1: A paddle has COM in the middle and DIT / DAH contacts on each side. It has no timing of its own
pgtelegraph.ponder.keyer.text_2: Wire it to the back of an electronic keyer: DIT to DIT, COM to COM, DAH to DAH. The keyer needs no supply
pgtelegraph.ponder.keyer.text_3: It closes its front OUT-OUT contact in correct Morse timing, 5-24 WPM on the front panel
pgtelegraph.ponder.keyer.text_4: Wire the keyer's two OUT terminals to the transmitter's KEY and COM - exactly where a straight key would go
pgtelegraph.ponder.keyer.text_5: Squeeze both paddles and dits and dahs alternate (iambic). R-click the paddle for focus mode: Z / X or the mouse buttons
pgtelegraph.ponder.keyer.text_6: A keyer paddle has the keyer built in: wire its two OUT terminals straight to KEY / COM. No supply, 5-40 WPM
pgtelegraph.ponder.keyer.text_7: Its contact is rated 30 V, 0.5 A - switch heavy loads through a relay
pgtelegraph.ponder.keyer.text_8: A clip key or clip paddle needs no block: its leads are insulated copper wire. Sneak R-click two terminals (KEY, then COM) to clip them on
pgtelegraph.ponder.paper_tape.text_1: A perforator punches a typed message into paper tape in Morse - letters, digits and Hangul. No power needed
pgtelegraph.ponder.paper_tape.text_2: A tape transmitter reads the tape with a star wheel and works its OUT contact
pgtelegraph.ponder.paper_tape.text_3: Its tape is pulled by Create rotation on the back, sides or bottom: RPM / 4 = WPM (64 RPM = 16 WPM)
pgtelegraph.ponder.paper_tape.text_4: Below 8 RPM it stalls, above 128 RPM the tape tears
pgtelegraph.ponder.paper_tape.text_5: Its OUT is a contact like a key: put it in a loop with a battery and an inker here, or across a transmitter's KEY / COM
pgtelegraph.ponder.paper_tape.text_6: An inker draws the marks on tape from 40 mA. Right-click the tape to read the decoded text
pgtelegraph.ponder.paper_tape.text_7: An inked tape can go back into a tape transmitter: it plays back as received at 48 RPM
pgtelegraph.ponder.vlf_station.text_1: An Alexanderson alternator makes RF by rotation alone - it is keyed through its KEY / COM terminals like a transmitter
pgtelegraph.ponder.vlf_station.text_2: Drive it with Create rotation on its back: frequency = RPM x 67.19 Hz (256 RPM = 17.2 kHz)
pgtelegraph.ponder.vlf_station.text_3: At VLF any mast is far too short. Wire alternator -> coax -> loading coil -> coax -> mast
pgtelegraph.ponder.vlf_station.text_4: Set the coil's inductance with an empty hand and watch resonance through Engineer's Goggles: the bandwidth is only about 100 Hz
pgtelegraph.ponder.vlf_station.text_5: Top-load wire from the mast top adds capacitance and effective height - about 3x the mast height is plenty
pgtelegraph.ponder.vlf_station.text_6: Ground mats within 24 blocks of the mast foot cut the ground loss - the biggest factor in VLF efficiency
pgtelegraph.ponder.vlf_station.text_7: The earth and the bottom of the ionosphere guide VLF like a pipe: it loses only 2-3 dB per 1000 km, day and night, and is heard thousands of km away
pgtelegraph.ponder.vlf_station.text_8: Keep the speed steady: a speed change moves the frequency off the antenna's resonance
pgtelegraph.ponder.beam_antennas.text_1: Yagi, helix and dish antennas are directional. They are placed pointing where you look; empty hand opens azimuth / elevation
pgtelegraph.ponder.beam_antennas.text_2: Or put a rotator under it and drive it with Create rotation from below: 100:1, 64 RPM is about one turn in 2.5 min
pgtelegraph.ponder.beam_antennas.text_3: The narrower the beam, the more exactly you must aim: yagi 12 dBi / 40 deg, dish about 38 dBi / 2 deg at 10 GHz
pgtelegraph.ponder.beam_antennas.text_4: Set the band on the antenna's side panel
pgtelegraph.ponder.beam_antennas.text_5: A receiving loop hears LF/VLF about as well as a huge antenna. Its deep null broadside finds a station's bearing (sneak R-click to turn it)
pgtelegraph.ponder.fm_broadcast.text_1: The blue FM broadcast transmitter has the FM band built in: 87.5-108 MHz, up to 1 kW, 250 V supply. Records and the microphone work as on the AM set
pgtelegraph.ponder.fm_broadcast.text_2: FM swings the frequency by up to 75 kHz with the sound: 15 kHz audio, clean and wide - a strong station has no static at all
pgtelegraph.ponder.fm_broadcast.text_3: VHF goes only as far as line of sight, so height is everything: the radio horizon is 4.12 x (sqrt h1 + sqrt h2) km. Put the antenna on a tower or a hill
pgtelegraph.ponder.fm_broadcast.text_4: Hills and buildings in the way cost a lot: the far side of a mountain hears little
pgtelegraph.ponder.fm_broadcast.text_5: A radio tuned above 30 MHz is an FM set: tune it to the station (sneak + empty hand)
pgtelegraph.ponder.fm_broadcast.text_6: Near the edge FM does not fade into hiss like AM: it stays clean, then crackles and drops out, and the radio turns a weak station down
pgtelegraph.ponder.fm_broadcast.text_7: Two stations on one frequency: the stronger captures the radio completely and the other vanishes (capture effect)
pgtelegraph.ponder.radio_parts.text_1: A freshly built radio is an empty case: it does nothing until its parts are fitted
pgtelegraph.ponder.radio_parts.text_2: R-click it with a screwdriver to open the parts bay. Engineer's Goggles list the parts still missing
pgtelegraph.ponder.radio_parts.text_3: A transmitter needs a fuse (20 A for 100 W), a power stage (PA: 10, 50 or 100 W) and a band module that covers the frequency
pgtelegraph.ponder.radio_parts.text_4: Optional: a low-pass filter stops harmonics (without one the 2nd harmonic is only 25 dB down); a TCXO, OCXO or GPSDO keeps the frequency from drifting
pgtelegraph.ponder.radio_parts.text_5: A receiver needs a fuse (2 A), a regulator, a low-noise amplifier (LNA), an IF filter and a band module
pgtelegraph.ponder.radio_parts.text_6: The IF filter sets what you hear: 250 or 500 Hz crystal for CW, 2.4 kHz ceramic for voice. The narrower, the less noise
pgtelegraph.ponder.radio_parts.text_7: Optional: an EMI filter keeps out the hash of nearby machines; a better LNA hears weaker signals
pgtelegraph.ponder.radio_parts.text_8: Broken up, a radio keeps its parts inside: carry it away and place it again as it was. Its tooltip lists them
pgtelegraph.ponder.radio_parts.text_9: A handheld opens its parts with the Parts button on its panel: battery, regulator, LNA, IF filter, power stage and band module
pgtelegraph.ponder.handheld.text_1: The handheld is a 2 m / 70 cm CW transceiver you carry: 0.5, 1 or 5 W into a rubber-duck antenna, a 7.4 V 14.8 Wh battery
pgtelegraph.ponder.handheld.text_2: Sneak R-click opens its panel: power, frequency, output, squelch - and the Parts button. A new one is empty: fit a battery, regulator, LNA, IF filter, power stage and band module
pgtelegraph.ponder.handheld.text_3: Hold R-click to send like a straight key; in paddle mode left click is dit and right click dah through the built-in keyer
pgtelegraph.ponder.handheld.text_4: It listens from anywhere in your inventory. VHF is line of sight: stand on high ground and it reaches much further
pgtelegraph.ponder.handheld.text_5: The charger docks it (R-click with the radio) and charges at about 10 W from a 12 V Power Grid supply: empty to full in about 1 h 45 min
pgtelegraph.ponder.handheld.text_6: Green light: charging. Red: the supply is too low (it needs 9 V or more). Empty hand takes the radio back
pgtelegraph.ponder.instruments.text_1: SWR / power meter: hold it and look at a transmitter - forward and reflected power and the SWR. Above about 2:1, retune or add a tuner
pgtelegraph.ponder.instruments.text_2: Field strength meter: hold it - all the RF arriving where you stand, every frequency. Quick check that an antenna radiates
pgtelegraph.ponder.instruments.text_3: Frequency counter: the frequency of the strongest signal here (above -90 dBm) - catches a drifting oscillator
pgtelegraph.ponder.instruments.text_4: Direction finder: hold it and sweep round - the signal peaks in its 40 degree beam toward the station. Sneak + use tunes it
pgtelegraph.ponder.instruments.text_5: Spectrum analyzer: use it to open a display of the band - every carrier, harmonics and the noise floor at a glance
pgtelegraph.ponder.instruments.text_6: Oscilloscope: two channels (CH1, CH2 +/-) on Power Grid wires, 1 MOhm inputs rated 1 kV, one sample a tick, the last 10 s on screen
pgtelegraph.ponder.coax_switch.text_1: A coax switch has a common port at its back and two ports: A on the left, B on the right
pgtelegraph.ponder.coax_switch.text_2: Run the radio into the common port and an antenna to each side - here two antennas for different bands
pgtelegraph.ponder.coax_switch.text_3: No redstone: A is connected. A redstone signal throws it to B - so the antennas can be chosen from far away
pgtelegraph.ponder.coax_switch.text_4: It works the other way round too: one antenna shared by two radios
pgtelegraph.ponder.spark.text_1: The way radio began (about 1900): a spark jumps a gap and rings the antenna like a struck bell. There is no oscillator
pgtelegraph.ponder.spark.text_2: It needs about 1 kV (at least 400 V; insulated to 3 kV), up to 2 kW on the panel, and only 25 % of that leaves as radio
pgtelegraph.ponder.spark.text_3: So the frequency is the antenna's own resonance - the dial does nothing. Lengthen the antenna or add a loading coil to move it
pgtelegraph.ponder.spark.text_4: The signal is smeared over 10 % of that frequency (at least 20 kHz): every receiver around hears a harsh rasp across the band
pgtelegraph.ponder.spark.text_5: That is why spark was banned and tuned transmitters took over - fun to build, but your neighbours will hear it
pgtelegraph.ponder.analog_tv.text_1: A TV transmitter sends the live picture of the TV camera touching it - the camera's real view, filmed by a nearby player's game at 640 x 480
pgtelegraph.ponder.analog_tv.text_2: It works on 54-890 MHz (the VHF and UHF TV bands), up to 1 kW from 250 V. INHIBIT shorted to COM takes it off the air
pgtelegraph.ponder.analog_tv.text_3: TV is VHF / UHF: line of sight. A high antenna covers far more ground
pgtelegraph.ponder.analog_tv.text_4: A TV set tuned to the channel shows it. Empty hand watches close up, sneak changes channel. Coax to an outside antenna beats its rabbit ears
pgtelegraph.ponder.analog_tv.text_5: A weak signal looks like real analog TV: snow, the colour fading out, lines tearing sideways and the picture rolling
pgtelegraph.ponder.analog_tv.text_6: Hills in the way add ghosts; another station on the same channel shows as moving bars
pgtelegraph.ponder.vcr.text_1: A VCR plays and records video tapes: 10 minutes each, 320 x 240 at 15 frames a second (about VHS)
pgtelegraph.ponder.vcr.text_2: Tape in hand, R-click: put it in. Empty hand: STOP > PLAY > LOOP > REC. Recording goes on after what is on the tape. Sneak + empty hand: eject.
pgtelegraph.ponder.vcr.text_3: Playing, its RF output puts the picture on channel 3 (61.25 MHz) at a microwatt: tune a TV set close by to it
pgtelegraph.ponder.vcr.text_4: REC records the TV set touching it - the picture as that set gets it, snow and ghosts included
pgtelegraph.ponder.vcr.text_5: A TV transmitter touching a playing VCR broadcasts the tape in place of a camera. LOOP keeps it going
pgtelegraph.ponder.vcr.text_6: A camcorder records what you see onto the tape inside it. Off hand tape + sneak R-click: load. R-click: record / stop
pgtelegraph.ponder.vcr.text_7: Video files on the server's machine go onto a held tape with /pgvideo import (and out as MP4 with /pgvideo export)
pgtelegraph.ponder.bodycam.text_1: A bodycam is the TV transmitter's partner: it films what its wearer sees and the transmitter puts it on the air
pgtelegraph.ponder.bodycam.text_2: Sneak + R-click the TV transmitter with it: they are paired
pgtelegraph.ponder.bodycam.text_3: Then wear it in the chest armour slot (R-click puts it on). Within 300 blocks of the transmitter it sends 640 x 480 at up to 30 frames a second
pgtelegraph.ponder.bodycam.text_4: With no TV camera touching the transmitter, the bodycam's picture is what goes out - watch it on any set on the channel
pgtelegraph.ponder.audio_pa.text_1: An audio amplifier plays the sound of the radio set touching it - a broadcast radio or a receiver
pgtelegraph.ponder.audio_pa.text_2: It runs off PWR+ / PWR- at the back: 1-2000 W out (front panel), 60 % efficient, 230 V nominal - less voltage, less power
pgtelegraph.ponder.audio_pa.text_3: Wire loudspeakers to its front SPK terminals; they share the output. A speaker: 92 dB at 1 m for 1 W, up to 100 W, broad
pgtelegraph.ponder.audio_pa.text_4: Driven past 1.5 times its rating for 5 s, a speaker burns its voice coil
pgtelegraph.ponder.audio_pa.text_5: A horn loudspeaker throws 112 dB per watt in a 15 degree beam from the mouth at its back - up to 600 W, heard kilometres away. Empty hand: tilt
pgtelegraph.ponder.audio_pa.text_6: Loudness falls 6 dB per doubling of distance and 5 dB a km to the air; sound arrives late by 1 s per 343 m
pgtelegraph.ponder.audio_pa.text_7: In front of a horn at full power it hurts: from 120 dB (about 10 m) you take damage, from 110 dB you feel sick. Walls and helmets help
pgtelegraph.ponder.jammer.text_1: A jammer sends noise, not a signal: its power spread over a bandwidth you choose (10 kHz - 50 MHz) round the dial
pgtelegraph.ponder.jammer.text_2: Receivers in that band hear no station - their noise floor rises and weak signals drown first. TV sets snow up, SSTV fills with grain, satellites stop taking commands
pgtelegraph.ponder.jammer.text_3: The narrower the band, the harder it hits: a tenth of the width is 10 dB more. Up to 1 kW from 250 V; INHIBIT shorted to COM switches it off
pgtelegraph.ponder.lna.text_1: A long coax run loses signal - and every dB it loses on VHF/UHF is a dB of signal-to-noise gone
pgtelegraph.ponder.lna.text_2: An in-line LNA right at the antenna lifts the signal 20 dB (noise figure 0.8 dB) before the coax can lose it: weak stations come up out of the hiss
pgtelegraph.ponder.lna.text_3: On HF the sky is noisier than any amplifier, so it gains nothing there
pgtelegraph.ponder.lna.text_4: It only amplifies towards the radio: transmit through it and it burns out at once. Give the transmitter its own antenna or a coax switch
item.pgtelegraph.fpv_goggles.tooltip.sum: An analog TV receiver worn on the head (_helmet slot_) with a small antenna on top. Tuned to a TV transmitter or a _bodycam's_ channel, the live picture _fills your view_ - with snow, colour loss, tearing and ghosts as the signal fades. Sneak + R-click: channel (50 MHz - 6 GHz). R-click: put them on; take them off to see again.
block.pgtelegraph.remote_tuner.tooltip.s: A weatherproof automatic tuner that goes _right at the antenna feed_: matches up to _SWR 100:1_ - short whips and random wires. Loss still grows with the mismatch (4 dB at 32:1, up to 10 dB), and any coax between it and the antenna runs at that huge SWR, so mount it _directly against the antenna_.
block.pgtelegraph.manual_tuner.tooltip.s: A roller inductor (_L_) and a variable capacitor (_C_) on the lid. It matches only around the frequency they resonate at, _f = 1/(2π√LC)_ (Engineer's Goggles show it and the antenna's SWR there). Range _64:1_ and less loss than an automatic tuner, but it holds narrower the worse the antenna is - retune it when you change band.
pgtelegraph.tuner.out: Antenna SWR there %s:1 - out of range (64:1)
pgtelegraph.video.erase_ask: Sneak + use again within 3 s to wipe this tape

pgtelegraph.supply.ionosonde.1: or plug a Power Grid power cord straight into it

pgtelegraph.supply.sstv_monitor.1: or plug a Power Grid power cord straight into it

pgtelegraph.supply.tv_receiver.1: or plug a Power Grid power cord straight into it
pgtelegraph.supply.tv_receiver.2: An antenna through coax (or a VCR nearby on channel 3)
pgtelegraph.supply.broadcast_radio.0: PWR+/PWR-: 13.8 V (works from 9.7 V, burns above 18 V), about 25 W (1.8 A)
pgtelegraph.supply.broadcast_radio.1: or plug a Power Grid power cord straight into it
pgtelegraph.supply.qso_robot.0: PWR+/PWR-: 13.8 V (works from 9.7 V, burns above 18 V), about 150 W
pgtelegraph.supply.qso_robot.1: or plug a Power Grid power cord straight into it
