pgtelegraph.supply.audio_amplifier.1: or plug a Power Grid power cord straight into it
pgtelegraph.supply.audio_amplifier.2: Sound in: a receiver or radio touching it (its own speaker goes quiet) or a microphone touching it
pgtelegraph.supply.audio_amplifier.3: SPK 1/SPK 2 to the speakers (several in parallel)
pgtelegraph.supply.speaker.0: To an amplifier's SPK 1/SPK 2 (cord or wire), or touching the amplifier
pgtelegraph.supply.speaker.1: Rated 100 W; 1.5 x for 5 s burns it
pgtelegraph.supply.horn_speaker.0: To an amplifier's SPK 1/SPK 2 (cord or wire), or touching the amplifier
pgtelegraph.supply.horn_speaker.1: Rated 600 W; 1.5 x for 5 s burns it
pgtelegraph.supply.jammer.0: PWR+/PWR-: 250 V DC (works from 120 V, max 600 V)
pgtelegraph.supply.jammer.1: About 10 A jamming at 1 kW (40 % efficient)
pgtelegraph.supply.microphone.1: Against a transmitter, broadcast transmitter or audio amplifier
pgtelegraph.supply.inline_lna.0: No supply needed (taken as fed up the coax)
pgtelegraph.supply.inline_lna.1: In the coax between antenna and receiver; transmit into it and it burns
block.pgtelegraph.power_supply.tooltip.s: A switch-mode supply that turns _90-300 V_ from the grid into the _13.8 V_ radios run on. Grid (or a power cord) to _IN_ at the back, 13.8 V equipment to _OUT_ at the front. Rated _30 A_ (about 400 W), 88 % efficient. Past _33 A_ it folds the voltage back to limit the current, so a short will not burn it, but more than _300 V_ in will.
pgtelegraph.psu.no_input: Input too low (needs 90 V or more)
pgtelegraph.supply.power_supply.0: IN+/IN-: 90-300 V (burns above 300 V), or a power cord
pgtelegraph.supply.transmitter.2: 13.8 V comes from a DC Power Supply's OUT
pgtelegraph.supply.beacon.2: 13.8 V comes from a DC Power Supply's OUT
pgtelegraph.supply.repeater.2: 13.8 V comes from a DC Power Supply's OUT
pgtelegraph.supply.sstv_transmitter.2: 13.8 V comes from a DC Power Supply's OUT
pgtelegraph.supply.receiver.1: 13.8 V comes from a DC Power Supply's OUT
pgtelegraph.supply.sstv_monitor.3: 13.8 V comes from a DC Power Supply's OUT
pgtelegraph.supply.broadcast_radio.3: 13.8 V comes from a DC Power Supply's OUT
pgtelegraph.supply.qso_robot.3: 13.8 V comes from a DC Power Supply's OUT
pgtelegraph.ponder.power_supply.text_1: A DC power supply turns anything from 90 to 300 V on the grid into the steady 13.8 V radios run on
pgtelegraph.ponder.power_supply.text_2: The grid goes on IN+ / IN- at the back - Power Grid wire, or a power cord plugged straight into the box
pgtelegraph.ponder.power_supply.text_3: 13.8 V equipment goes on OUT+ / OUT- at the front: transmitters, receivers, radios, the SSTV receiver - several in parallel
pgtelegraph.ponder.power_supply.text_4: Rated 30 A (about 400 W), 88 % efficient. Past 33 A it folds the voltage back, so a short will not burn it - but more than 300 V in will
pgtelegraph.ponder.power_supply.text_5: Power Grid is all DC: 230 V boxes like the TV set, the ionosonde or the audio amplifier take the grid directly
pgtelegraph.ponder.manual_tuner.text_1: A manual tuner goes in the coax between the rig and the antenna. Its two knobs set a roller inductor L and a variable capacitor C
pgtelegraph.ponder.manual_tuner.text_2: It matches only around f = 1/(2π√LC): turn the knobs (scroll on them) until that is your operating frequency
pgtelegraph.ponder.manual_tuner.text_3: The meter on the lid shows the SWR the rig sees at its own frequency: tune for the dip, left is 1:1, the red end is past 3:1
pgtelegraph.ponder.manual_tuner.text_4: It matches up to 64:1 and loses less than an automatic tuner, but the further off the antenna is, the narrower the match - change band, retune
pgtelegraph.ponder.manual_tuner.text_5: Automatic tuners need no hands: a desk tuner matches up to 10:1, a remote tuner right at the antenna up to 100:1
pgtelegraph.ponder.wall_coax.text_1: Coax laid on the floor runs like redstone. Click the side of a block with it and it clips to the wall instead
pgtelegraph.ponder.wall_coax.text_2: Wall coax runs straight up and down the wall, and sideways along it; the floor run joins it at the bottom
pgtelegraph.ponder.wall_coax.text_3: At the top it goes over onto the roof and on to the antenna - one block of cable is still one metre of loss
pgtelegraph.ponder.antenna_stacking.head: Stacking beam antennas
pgtelegraph.ponder.antenna_stacking.text: More of the same kind on the same band, aimed the same way (within about 10°) and within 2 blocks of each other, work as one stack - feeding one feeds them all
Each doubling adds about 3 dB of gain (10·log N, less 0.4 dB of phasing loss) and the beam narrows by √N - up to 16 antennas, side by side or one above another
They want to be about 0.6 wavelengths apart: packed closer, they overlap and give less
Yagis, dishes and helices stack this way
pgtelegraph.ponder.manpack.text_1: R-click puts the manpack on your back (chest armour slot) - other players see it, whip and all
pgtelegraph.ponder.manpack.text_2: Sneak R-click opens its panel: power, frequency, output 1 / 5 / 10 / 20 W, squelch - and the parts, the same as a handheld
pgtelegraph.ponder.manpack.text_3: Hold V (push to talk) and speak: it goes out as NFM voice, and whoever is on the frequency comes back through the earpiece, noise and squelch included
pgtelegraph.ponder.manpack.text_4: The 1 m whip above your shoulder and the bigger power stage reach several times further than a handheld
pgtelegraph.ponder.fpv_goggles.text_1: A TV camera into a TV transmitter puts a live picture on the air
pgtelegraph.ponder.fpv_goggles.text_2: FPV goggles are a TV receiver worn on the head (helmet slot). Sneak R-click sets the channel, 50 MHz - 6 GHz - the transmitter's or a bodycam's
pgtelegraph.ponder.fpv_goggles.text_3: Put them on (R-click) and the picture fills your view, with snow, colour loss and tearing as the signal fades. Take them off to see again
pgtelegraph.ponder.pa_microphone.text_1: A microphone touching an audio amplifier makes a public address: hold V and your voice comes out of every speaker on the line
pgtelegraph.ponder.pa_microphone.text_2: A radio touching the amplifier plays through the speakers only - its own speaker goes quiet
pgtelegraph.ponder.pa_microphone.text_3: Talk over the music and it ducks under your voice, then comes back up when you stop
pgtelegraph.ponder.pa_microphone.text_4: All the speakers on one amplifier play in step: only the distance to each one makes a difference
block.pgtelegraph.ups.tooltip.summary: A 13.8 V supply with batteries inside (_500 Wh_). With the grid up it runs the station and charges at up to _120 W_; when IN drops below _90 V_ the batteries take over without a break. It beeps every 5 s while on battery. Otherwise the same as the DC Power Supply (30 A, current limit at 33 A, burns above 300 V).
pgtelegraph.supply.ups.0: IN+/IN-: 90-300 V (burns above 300 V), or a power cord
pgtelegraph.supply.ups.1: OUT+/OUT-: 13.8 V, up to 30 A, carries on through a blackout
pgtelegraph.supply.ups.2: About 4.5 hours on battery at 100 W
block.pgtelegraph.dtmf_decoder.tooltip.s: A DTMF decoder with its own FM receiver. Put an antenna on its coax and _set the frequency_: it recognises touch-tone digits on it and gives out a _redstone signal_ (a receiver right next to it is used instead, if there is one). Send the code from the keypad on a handheld or manpack panel to switch far-away doors and machines. Runs on 13.8 V (2 W).
pgtelegraph.supply.dtmf_decoder.0: PWR+/PWR-: 13.8 V (works from 9.7 V, burns above 18 V), 2 W
pgtelegraph.supply.dtmf_decoder.1: An antenna on its coax (or an AM/FM/SSB receiver right next to it)
pgtelegraph.supply.dtmf_decoder.2: 13.8 V comes from a DC Power Supply's OUT
pgtelegraph.dtmf.hint.0: The ON code gives signal 15 for one second
pgtelegraph.dtmf.hint.1: With no OFF code the ON code toggles
block.pgtelegraph.creative_transmitter.t: A test transmitter that needs no supply and no parts and never burns (nor does its coax). The power box opens a board with a row per multiplier _x1 / x10 / x100 / x1000_, 1-250 in each: up to _250 kW_. Keyed like the normal one (KEY terminals, microphone, computer) and also by a _redstone signal_.
block.pgtelegraph.creative_receiver.tool: A test receiver that needs no supply and no parts and never burns. Any frequency, an ideal low-noise front end. Modes, filters and CTCSS as on the normal receiver.
block.pgtelegraph.power_panel.tooltip.su: Splits one 13.8 V feed into _four separately fused outputs_. An output that draws more than its fuse blows only that fuse; the others stay live. Bus rated 40 A.
pgtelegraph.supply.power_panel.0: IN+: 13.8 V (a supply or UPS OUT+), GND: common negative
pgtelegraph.supply.power_panel.1: OUT1-OUT4 to the sets' PWR+, their PWR- to GND
block.pgtelegraph.equipment_rack.tooltip: A steel rack frame that joins up and down. _Right-click it with a box-type device to mount the device in that cell_: it sits shallow in the frame, its wire terminals move to a _strip on the back_ and its coax goes on the _back only_. Coax behind different units never joins, so every radio keeps its own antenna. Mount a _power distribution panel_ in the same rack group and 13.8 V units get their power wiring laid automatically. Racks and mounted units are one piece of metal: ground one and the whole group - and every lightning arrester touching it - is grounded.
block.pgtelegraph.aprs_station.tooltip.s: Receives _APRS position reports_ on 144.390 MHz and plots them on a map. The items in the _two frequency slots_ on top make its network key: only trackers and vehicle radios with the same key show up. Needs an antenna on its coax and 13.8 V (10 W).
block.pgtelegraph.aprs_station.tooltip.b: Set the network key (not used up; sneak + empty hand clears)
Copy the key into the tracker
pgtelegraph.supply.aprs_station.0: PWR+/PWR-: 13.8 V (works from 9.7 V, burns above 18 V), 10 W
pgtelegraph.supply.aprs_station.1: A 2 m antenna on its coax (144.390 MHz)
pgtelegraph.supply.aprs_station.2: 13.8 V comes from a DC Power Supply's OUT
pgtelegraph.aprs.copied: Network key copied into the tracker
block.pgtelegraph.mobile_radio.tooltip.s: A _50 W_ set for Create trains, carts and airships. _Riding_ a contraption that carries one, your handheld or manpack transmits through its 50 W and roof antenna, on the vehicle's power instead of its battery. Parked or moving, it also sends the vehicle's _APRS position_ every 30 s.
pgtelegraph.mobile.hint: Put it on a contraption and ride it: your radio transmits at 50 W. A name tag names it
pgtelegraph.supply.sstv_monitor.4: Also takes 137 MHz weather-satellite APT: NOAA-15 137.620, NOAA-18 137.9125, NOAA-19 137.100 MHz
pgtelegraph.supply.repeater.3: CTCSS button on the dial screen: only relays signals carrying that tone
block.pgtelegraph.qso_robot.tooltip.cond: Mode button on the dial screen
pgtelegraph.contest.no_exchange: No exchange: put the report and the serial you got in the RST box, e.g. "5NN 012"
pgtelegraph.logbook.score: %s QSOs · %s mults · %s dupes · %s without exchange -> score %s
block.pgtelegraph.field_phone.tooltip.su: A magneto field telephone after the EE-8. Wire _L1 / L2_ to the other phone with two wires (or one wire and L2 to earth). Turning the crank puts about _75 V_ on the line: the bell at the far end rings and a switchboard's drop falls. Lift the handset and talk with _push-to-talk (V)_: your voice goes along the wires to every phone that is off the hook - through switchboards only along their cords - with more hiss on longer lines.
block.pgtelegraph.field_phone.tooltip.be: Turn the magneto crank (ring the far end)
pgtelegraph.supply.field_phone.0: L1 / L2: to the other phone or a switchboard line (no supply needed)
pgtelegraph.supply.field_phone.1: With a single wire, L2 to a grounding rod (earth return)
block.pgtelegraph.duplex_set.tooltip.sum: A bridge duplex: _both ends send at once_ over one wire. The key puts 60 V on a Wheatstone bridge whose one arm goes to the line and the other to an _artificial line_ (a rheostat). The receiving relay sits between them, so with the artificial line matched to the real one _your own sending leaves your relay still and only the far end moves it_. Balance it with the value box on top.
pgtelegraph.supply.duplex_set.0: LINE: the line, EARTH: a grounding rod (earth return)
pgtelegraph.supply.duplex_set.1: KEY / KEY COM: telegraph key, OUT / OUT: sounder + local battery
pgtelegraph.supply.duplex_set.2: Both ends need a duplex set
pgtelegraph.duplex.balanced: Balanced: your sending leaves your relay still
pgtelegraph.duplex.unbalanced: Out of balance (or the far end is sending too)
A Wheatstone bridge and megger for finding faults. Wire LINE to the line and EARTH to a ground rod and press it (empty hand): for 2 s it puts 10 V on and measures the _resistance from line to earth_ - an open line reads very high, a leak or earth fault low. It also walks the line and gives the length of wire to _every device, every break, every wet leaking insulator_.
pgtelegraph.supply.line_test_set.0: LINE: the line under test, EARTH: a grounding rod
block.pgtelegraph.submarine_cable.toolti: A long submarine cable with the sea as its return, all in one block (_10-4000 km_, value box): _3 Ω_ and _0.25 μF_ to the sea per km, so a pulse put in at one end comes out of the other _rounded, late and weak_. The longer, the slower you must send - the trouble of the 1858 Atlantic cable. Read the far end with a _mirror galvanometer_, not a sounder.
pgtelegraph.supply.submarine_cable.0: A / B: the two shore ends. The sea is the return (no supply)
pgtelegraph.supply.submarine_cable.1: Send several times slower than the RC time in the goggles
block.pgtelegraph.mirror_galvanometer.to: Thomson's galvanometer: a tiny magnet and mirror on a silk thread in a 50 Ω coil, showing _a few microamps_. A _spot of light_ on the scale in front swings with the current. Past the _trip level (20 μA - 5 mA)_ in the + direction its contact closes, so it can work a local sounder or inker like a relay.
pgtelegraph.supply.mirror_galvanometer.0: IN+ / IN-: between the cable end and earth
block.pgtelegraph.telegraph_repeater.too: An automatic repeater for the middle of a long line. Current from the WEST pulls the west relay, which puts a _fresh 120 V battery_ on the east line, and the other way round. While one side is repeating the other relay is locked out, so it does not _latch on its own output_. Pick-up current: value box.
pgtelegraph.supply.telegraph_repeater.0: WEST / EAST: the two lines, EARTH: a grounding rod
pgtelegraph.vna.hint: Right-click a radio, tuner or coax: sweeps the antenna behind it, 101 points (SWR, return loss, Smith chart, R + jX)
pgtelegraph.switchboard.need_wire: Hold insulated copper wire to plug in a cord
pgtelegraph.patchcord.hint: Lay it like insulated copper wire. To take it off, no wire cutter: right-click a terminal one of its plugs sits in, with an empty hand or anything, and the whole cord comes back to your inventory.
block.pgtelegraph.line_simulator.tooltip: A test block: A and B behave as if joined by an overhead line of the _set length (1 m - 250 km)_ - its wire resistance and insulator leakage (much worse in rain) - and the line test set and field telephone count the distance too. Length: the value box on top (rows x1 / x10 / x100 / x1000).
Wire kind (iron telegraph wire 8 Ω/km / copper 3 Ω/km)
pgtelegraph.ponder.ups_power_panel.text_: The UPS is the 13.8 V power supply with 500 Wh of batteries inside. With the grid up it runs the station and charges
When IN drops below 90 V the batteries take over without a break, and it beeps every 5 seconds. The goggles show the charge and the time left
A distribution panel splits one 13.8 V feed into four outputs, each with its own blade fuse
Each set takes an OUT on its PWR+, and every PWR- goes back to GND. A short on one output blows only that fuse - the rest stay on
Empty hand: new fuses for the blown ones. Sneak: the fuse size, 5 / 10 / 20 / 30 A. A blown fuse makes the lamp blink
pgtelegraph.ponder.equipment_rack.text_1: Equipment racks stack into one steel frame. Right-click a rack with a box-type device to mount it there, shallow, with its terminals and coax port moved to the back
pgtelegraph.ponder.equipment_rack.text_2: Racks that touch are one piece of metal: ground any one of them - a grounding rod or a ground mat - and the whole group is ground
pgtelegraph.ponder.equipment_rack.text_3: A lightning arrester touching any rack of a grounded group counts as grounded - no separate ground wire for each
pgtelegraph.ponder.dtmf_decoder.text_1: A DTMF decoder has its own FM receiver: an antenna on its coax, the frequency set in its screen (empty hand)
pgtelegraph.ponder.dtmf_decoder.text_2: Press keys on a handheld or manpack panel: each press keys the radio for a short touch-tone burst on its frequency
pgtelegraph.ponder.dtmf_decoder.text_3: The right code gives a redstone signal on every side: a 1 s pulse, a latch with ON / OFF codes, or the last digit as its strength
pgtelegraph.ponder.dtmf_decoder.text_4: It runs on 13.8 V. A receiver placed right against it is used instead of its own
pgtelegraph.ponder.aprs.text_1: An APRS station listens on 144.390 MHz and plots every position report it decodes on a map (empty hand)
pgtelegraph.ponder.aprs.text_2: The two slots on top are its network key, set like a redstone link's frequency: only reports with the same two items show up
pgtelegraph.ponder.aprs.text_3: Right-click the station with an APRS tracker to copy the key. Switched on, the tracker sends your position every 30 s from your inventory
pgtelegraph.ponder.aprs.text_4: A vehicle radio on a train, cart or airship reports the vehicle's position, and riders' radios transmit through it at 50 W
pgtelegraph.ponder.field_phone.text_1: Field telephones talk over a pair of wires (or one wire with L2 to earth). No supply is needed
pgtelegraph.ponder.field_phone.text_2: Sneak + empty hand turns the magneto crank: about 75 V on the line rings the bell at the far end
pgtelegraph.ponder.field_phone.text_3: Empty hand lifts the handset. Hold push-to-talk (V) and speak: your voice reaches every phone off the hook on the line
pgtelegraph.ponder.field_phone.text_4: Through a switchboard the voice follows only the cords plugged in - cords are insulated copper wire or patch cords
pgtelegraph.ponder.field_phone.text_5: A patch cord goes on like insulated wire, but comes off by hand: right-click the terminal its plug is in
pgtelegraph.ponder.duplex_set.text_1: A duplex set lets both ends send at the same time over one wire with earth return
pgtelegraph.ponder.duplex_set.text_2: LINE to the line, EARTH to a grounding rod, the key on KEY / KEY COM, a sounder with its local battery on OUT
pgtelegraph.ponder.duplex_set.text_3: Inside is a Wheatstone bridge: one arm to the line, the other to an artificial line (the value box). The relay sits across it
pgtelegraph.ponder.duplex_set.text_4: Turn the artificial line until your own key no longer moves your relay - the goggles say "balanced". Then only the far end works it
pgtelegraph.ponder.line_testing.text_1: A line test set: LINE to the line under test (a patch cord makes a handy test lead), EARTH to a grounding rod
pgtelegraph.ponder.line_testing.text_2: Press it: for 2 s it puts 10 V on and measures line-to-earth resistance. Open lines read very high, leaks and earth faults low
pgtelegraph.ponder.line_testing.text_3: It also walks the line: metres of wire to every device, every break and every wet, leaking insulator - in chat and in the goggles
pgtelegraph.ponder.line_testing.text_4: For testing without kilometres of poles: the creative line simulator acts as a line of the set length, 1 m to 250 km
pgtelegraph.ponder.line_testing.text_5: Its wire resistance and insulator leakage (much worse in rain) are real, and the tester and telephones count its length
pgtelegraph.ponder.submarine_cable.text_: A submarine cable block holds a whole cable, 10 to 4000 km long, with the sea as its return
Every km has 3 Ω and 0.25 μF to the sea: a pulse comes out the far end rounded, late and weak - the longer, the worse
Read it with a mirror galvanometer: a spot of light swings across its scale with a few microamps
Past its trip level its contact closes and can work a local sounder. Send slower than the cable's RC time (goggles) or the dots run together
pgtelegraph.ponder.telegraph_repeater.te: On a very long line the current is too weak to work a sounder. A repeater in the middle sends it on with a fresh 120 V battery
Current from the WEST line pulls the west relay, which puts the battery on the EAST line - and the other way round
While one side is repeating, the other side's relay is locked out so it cannot latch on its own output. Pick-up current: value box
pgtelegraph.ponder.creative_radio.text_1: Creative sets need no supply and no parts and never burn - for testing a station
pgtelegraph.ponder.creative_radio.text_2: The transmitter's power box has a row for each multiplier x1 / x10 / x100 / x1000, 1-250 in each: up to 250 kW
pgtelegraph.ponder.creative_radio.text_3: Besides its KEY terminals, a microphone or a computer, a redstone signal keys it too
pgtelegraph.ponder.creative_radio.text_4: A VNA on a radio, tuner or coax sweeps the antenna behind it: SWR, return loss, a Smith chart and R + jX at the marker
block.pgtelegraph.creative_antenna.toolt: A test antenna: _SWR 1:1 on every frequency_, no loss of its own, a 2.15 dBi omni pattern. Its height is not where it stands but its _value box (1-2500 m, rows x1 / x10)_ - for trying out paths. The coax to it still has its loss.
pgtelegraph.ponder.creative_radio.text_5: A creative antenna is matched on every frequency with no loss of its own; its value box sets how high it counts as, 1 to 2500 m
block.pgtelegraph.equipment_rack.tooltip: Mounts it in that cell (breaking gives back both the device and the rack)
